turns.query: I calibrate the oxygen sensor in air at the truck and then the pod goes into brackish water. What do I actually have to have right at the truck for that calibration to mean anything once it's in the water?

relevant.evidence:
The main goal of the one-point
DO calibration procedure is to create a 100-percent saturated
oxygen environment in which the DO sensor and its thermistor
are at the same temperature.
relevant.locator: Section 2.2 Calibration of Optical Sensors — "One-point calibration" / "Two-point calibration"

relevant.evidence:
Read the temperature to the nearest
0.1 degree Celsius (°C).
relevant.locator: Procedure 1—Calibration in Air — "Wet the inside of the calibration chamber"

relevant.evidence:
water droplets on the
sensor module or on the temperature sensor can cause
improper calibration.
relevant.locator: Procedure 1—Calibration in Air, steps 7–9 / Variation of Procedure 1 — "within ±0.2 mg/L or 2 percent of the computed saturation value"

relevant.evidence:
Place the wrapped sensor into the plastic bag and
keep it out of direct sunlight to keep the temperature
from changing.
relevant.locator: Variation of Procedure 1—Air Calibration with a Wet Towel / Procedure 2 introduction — "Place the wrapped sensor into the plastic bag"

relevant.evidence:
DO calibration procedures include corrections for
atmospheric pressure and ionic strength. (Ionic strength is
estimated from the conductivity measurement for routine field
applications.)
relevant.locator: Section 2.2.1 Correction for Atmospheric Pressure and Salinity / Technical Note 2 — "DO sensors do not directly measure oxygen in milligrams per liter"

relevant.evidence:
instruments have a built-in conductivity sensor that is used
to correct the DO-concentration data for salinity automatically.
For instruments that are not equipped with a conductivity
sensor
relevant.locator: Section 2.2.1 Correction for Atmospheric Pressure and Salinity / 2.2.2 Selection of Calibration Method — "It is required that the barometric pressure be measured at the altitude of the DO calibration"

relevant.evidence:
Most multiparameter instruments that
include DO and specific-conductance sensors automatically
correct the DO reading for salinity if needed, unless the fea-
ture is turned off by the user.
relevant.locator: Section 3.3 step 11-12, Section 4.0 Reporting, and Section 5.0 opening — "reported to the nearest 0.1 mg/L and stored to the nearest 0.01 mg/L"

relevant.evidence:
Temperature stability during calibration and
measurement is extremely important, as temperature controls
the solubility of oxygen in water.
relevant.locator: Section 2.1.1 Equipment Description and Maintenance — "Guidance on when to replace the luminophore-containing cap"
